newsitem.title: USA: New Magellan Fund manager describes strategy.
newsitem.headline: New Magellan Fund manager describes strategy.

text.p: The new manager of Fidelity Investments' Magellan Fund said on Thursday running a $54 billion fund took some getting used to.
Bob Stansky, who took over Magellan last June, told fund holders at a meeting in Boston it took time to adjust compared to his previous fund, Fidelity Growth Company Fund.
"$15 billion is not $55 billion, I'll be the first to admit. It took a little time to get used to it, yes," he said.

Responding to questions from an audience of about 2,000, Gary Burkhead, president of Fidelity Management and Research Corp, said Magellan's $54 billion in assets had not hurt the fund's performance, however.

Stansky cut back on Magellan's heavy exposure to bonds and cash when he took over the post to 7.9 percent of total assets in bonds and 3.6 percent in cash as of November 30, the most recent date figures are available.
He told the audience the portfolio was "fully invested in equities" but did not elaborate.

In an interview in a Fidelity brochure handed out to the audience, he said, "I've looked at the combination of cash and bonds in this low-interest rate environment and I think it's safe to say that my target is to be about five percent total non-equities."
Stansky said he thought bank stocks could benefit from mergers and acquisitions in the near term.
"I think we'll see a lot of acquisitions going forward," he said. The quickest way for banks to improve their revenues was to merge with another bank and then cut overhead costs, he said.
Magellan had 8.7 percent of its assets at the end of November invested in finance stocks, up from 5.8 percent at the end of May.
Stansky said Magellan was being run in the same way that previous managers such as Peter Lynch and Morris Smith ran the fund, by buying companies whose earnings were growing consistently.
Burkhead said Stansky had done "a really good job in repositioning" Magellan.
"I think that fund is well positioned for 1997," he said.
